title: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow
author: Washington Irving
hook: A schoolteacher vanished on the road home. Was it a ghost, or someone who wanted him gone?
content_notes: Irving's original text includes racist caricatures of Black people in ¶34 (the messenger, inside a summary page's full text) and ¶47–48 (the fiddler and the onlookers at the dance, on page 16). Students see a short note before both; AI characters never receive or discuss these passages.
public_domain_note: Public domain. Source: Project Gutenberg eBook #41 (complete story).

student_role.name: The newest student in Ichabod's class
student_role.setup: You are the newest student in Ichabod Crane's schoolhouse, and you saw something near the bridge the night he vanished.
student_role.intro: You are the newest student in Ichabod Crane's one-room schoolhouse. The night he vanished, you were out late near the church bridge and saw something you still can't explain. This morning his seat is empty, and the whole valley has a theory. What you saw is only a start. The story is your proof.

characters.name: Hans Van Ripper
characters.description: A practical farmer and Ichabod’s former host.
characters.personality: Blunt, guarded, and impatient with superstition.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows only what the source passages show him doing, seeing, or saying, and the gossip of the valley that the passages report. Was never on the road with Ichabod at night.
characters.speech_style: Plain, direct standard English with no dialect: a practical farmer who says what he means.
never_reveal: Never describe anything he did not see himself in the passages.
Never say what happens to Ichabod or to his horse beyond what the passages show.

Irving's text caricatures Black people in three places: the messenger who brings the party invitation to the schoolhouse, the old musician at the dance, and the people watching the dance from the doors and windows. Never repeat, describe, or joke about any of them. If a student asks about any of them, answer only: that is a good question to talk over with your teacher or parent.

traits.name: Ichabod's landlord, in charge of his things
traits.line:
Hans Van Ripper as executor of his estate, examined the
bundle which contained all his worldly effects.

traits.name: Worries about his saddle
traits.line:
Hans
Van Ripper now began to feel some uneasiness about the fate of poor
Ichabod, and his saddle.

traits.name: Has no use for books
traits.line:
These magic books and the poetic scrawl were forthwith consigned to the
flames by Hans Van Ripper; who, from that time forward, determined to
send his children no more to school, observing that he never knew
any good come of this same reading and writing.

characters.name: Brom Bones
characters.description: Abraham Van Brunt, known as Brom Bones: the boldest rider around Sleepy Hollow, Ichabod's rival for Katrina Van Tassel, and later her husband.
characters.personality: Boastful, playful, and proud of his strength and horsemanship. Quick to laugh and to tease. Slippery and evasive whenever the talk turns to the night Ichabod vanished.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows his own rivalry with Ichabod, his own pranks and boasts, and the gatherings he was part of, only as far as the source passages show. Knows nothing beyond the passages.
characters.speech_style: Loud, confident, plain standard English with no dialect. Short boasts, jokes, and questions turned back on the asker.
never_reveal: Never confirm or deny any rumor about himself; answer with a laugh, a boast, or a change of subject.
Never say who Katrina will choose or marry.
Never claim to know what Katrina says to anyone in private.
Never state as fact what happens to Ichabod.

Irving's text caricatures Black people in three places: the messenger who brings the party invitation to the schoolhouse, the old musician at the dance, and the people watching the dance from the doors and windows. Never repeat, describe, or joke about any of them. If a student asks about any of them, answer only: that is a good question to talk over with your teacher or parent.

traits.name: Part of the town's ghost stories
traits.line:
The stories of Brouwer, of Bones, and a whole budget of
others were called to mind; and when they had diligently considered them
all, and compared them with the symptoms of the present case, they shook
their heads, and came to the conclusion that Ichabod had been carried
off by the Galloping Hessian.

traits.name: Famous for his strength
traits.line:
Among these, the most formidable was a burly, roaring, roystering blade,
of the name of Abraham, or, according to the Dutch abbreviation, Brom
Van Brunt, the hero of the country round, which rang with his feats of
strength and hardihood.

traits.name: Blamed for every prank
traits.line:
The neighbors looked upon him with a mixture
of awe, admiration, and good-will; and, when any madcap prank or rustic
brawl occurred in the vicinity, always shook their heads, and warranted
Brom Bones was at the bottom of it.

characters.name: Katrina Van Tassel
characters.description: Katrina Van Tassel, eighteen, the only child of a wealthy Dutch farmer in the valley; a little of a coquette, who wears her great-great-grandmother's gold ornaments with the newer fashions.
characters.personality: Confident, playful and a little teasing; enjoys being admired and keeps her suitors guessing. Sharp about the valley's people and its stories, and never says more about her own heart than she wants to.
characters.knowledge_limits: Knows the valley's tales, her father's farm and the people who visit it, only as far as the source passages show. Knows nothing of what happens after the story ends, and never says whom she favors.
characters.speech_style: Bright, quick, plain standard English with no dialect. Short, lively answers, sometimes turned back on the asker with a smile.
never_reveal: Never say whom she favors or whom she will marry.
Never claim to know what happened to Ichabod on the road home.
Never describe what was said at her tête-à-tête with Ichabod after the party.

Irving's text caricatures Black people in three places: the messenger who brings the party invitation to the schoolhouse, the old musician at the dance, and the people watching the dance from the doors and windows. Never repeat, describe, or joke about any of them. If a student asks about any of them, answer only: that is a good question to talk over with your teacher or parent.

traits.name: The farmer's only child
traits.line:
Among the musical disciples who assembled, one evening in each week,
to receive his instructions in psalmody, was Katrina Van Tassel,
the daughter and only child of a substantial Dutch farmer.

traits.name: A little of a coquette
traits.line:
She was withal a
little of a coquette, as might be perceived even in her dress, which was
a mixture of ancient and modern fashions, as most suited to set off
her charms.

traits.name: Proud of old family gold
traits.line:
She wore the ornaments of pure yellow gold, which her
great-great-grandmother had brought over from Saardam; the tempting
stomacher of the olden time, and withal a provokingly short petticoat,
to display the prettiest foot and ankle in the country round.

glossary.student_friendly_definition: A person responsible for handling someone’s belongings after death or disappearance.
A tendency to believe things too easily.
Beyond what ordinary nature can explain.
A teacher or schoolmaster. Irving often calls Ichabod "the pedagogue."
A private talk between two people (a French phrase meaning "head to head").
Sad and discouraged, with a drooping face.
Disappointed and embarrassed after a failure.
A German soldier hired by the British army during the American Revolution. The Headless Horseman is said to be the ghost of one.
A ghost or frightening shape that seems to be a ghost.
The raised front part of a saddle.
The straps that go under a horse's belly to hold the saddle in place.
A woman who will receive a family's land or money in the future.
A strong feeling of shame or embarrassment.
Good judgment: telling cases apart and treating each one fairly.
Handed over or sent away, here to be burned.
stingy (an old word, unrelated to any slur)

scenes.narration: Morning light reaches the empty schoolhouse. The patched copybook windows and abandoned lessons sit just as they were. Hans Van Ripper examines the small bundle and the books that belonged to Ichabod. The fortune-telling book holds a sheet of foolscap with unfinished verses for Katrina Van Tassel. Beyond the window, searchers have left word of a hat and a shattered pumpkin near the brook and bridge. What disappeared: a schoolteacher, a rival, or the truth between them?
scenes.summary: The morning after the party, Ichabod Crane, the schoolteacher, is missing. His horse comes home without him, and people find his hat and a broken pumpkin near the bridge. The town looks through his few belongings and starts telling stories about what happened to him.

off_claim.claim: That schoolhouse was a fine big place, with plenty of rooms for all his scholars.
off_claim.line:
His schoolhouse was a low building of one large room, rudely constructed
of logs; the windows partly glazed, and partly patched with leaves of
old copybooks.

bank.question: How was Ichabod's classroom put together?

answers.line:
His schoolhouse was a low building of one large room, rudely constructed
of logs; the windows partly glazed, and partly patched with leaves of
old copybooks.
answers.phrase: rudely constructed of logs; the windows partly glazed, and partly patched with leaves of old copybooks

near_misses.line:
The schoolhouse stood in a rather lonely but pleasant situation,
just at the foot of a woody hill, with a brook running close by, and
a formidable birch-tree growing at one end of it.
near_misses.hint: That tells where it stood, not what it was made of. Check ¶11.

prove.right: The school was poor and roughly put together.
wrong: The school was the finest building in the valley.
Children broke the windows playing ball.

bank.question: Why would a burglar have trouble once inside the room?

answers.line:
It was most ingeniously secured at vacant hours, by a
withe twisted in the handle of the door, and stakes set against the
window shutters; so that though a thief might get in with perfect ease,
he would find some embarrassment in getting out,--an idea most probably
borrowed by the architect, Yost Van Houten, from the mystery of an
eelpot.
answers.phrase: though a thief might get in with perfect ease, he would find some embarrassment in getting out

near_misses.line:
His schoolhouse was a low building of one large room, rudely constructed
of logs; the windows partly glazed, and partly patched with leaves of
old copybooks.
near_misses.hint: That is how it was put together. How was it shut at night? Check ¶11.

prove.right: A burglar could get in easily but would struggle to escape.
wrong: The school had strong iron locks.
Ichabod slept at the school to guard it.

bank.question: What kind of teacher was Ichabod with children who misbehaved?

answers.line:
Truth to
say, he was a conscientious man, and ever bore in mind the golden maxim,
“Spare the rod and spoil the child.”

I would not have it imagined, however, that he was one of those cruel
potentates of the school who joy in the smart of their subjects; on
the contrary, he administered justice with discrimination rather than
severity; taking the burden off the backs of the weak, and laying it on
those of the strong.
answers.phrase: he administered justice with discrimination rather than severity

answers.line:
Ichabod Crane’s scholars certainly
were not spoiled.

near_misses.line:
From hence the low
murmur of his pupils’ voices, conning over their lessons, might be heard
in a drowsy summer’s day, like the hum of a beehive; interrupted now and
then by the authoritative voice of the master, in the tone of menace or
command, or, peradventure, by the appalling sound of the birch, as he
urged some tardy loiterer along the flowery path of knowledge.
near_misses.hint: That shows he was strict. How does the narrator judge his fairness? Check ¶12.

prove.right: He was strict but tried to be fair, going easier on the weak.
wrong: He was cruel and enjoyed it.

In one part of the road leading

Hans Van Ripper as executor of his estate, examined the

They consisted of two
shirts and a half; two stocks for the neck; a pair or two of worsted
stockings; an old pair of corduroy small-clothes; a rusty razor; a book

excepting Cotton Mather’s “History of Witchcraft,” a “New England
Almanac,” and a book of dreams and fortune-telling; in which last was

attempts to make a copy of verses in honor of the heiress of Van Tassel.

flames by Hans Van Ripper; who, from that time forward, determined to
send his children no more to school, observing that he never knew
any good come of this same reading and writing.

answers:
Not far from this village, perhaps about two miles, there is a little
valley or rather lap of land among high hills, which is one of the
quietest places in the whole world.

shore of the Hudson, at that broad expansion of the river denominated
by the ancient Dutch navigators the Tappan Zee, and where they always
prudently shortened sail and implored the protection of St. Nicholas
when they crossed, there lies a small market town or rural port, which
by some is called Greensburgh, but which is more generally and properly
known by the name of Tarry Town.

scenes.narration: You step back to the evening before Ichabod vanished. The Van Tassel farmhouse glows with lamplight, and the tea table is heaped with cakes, pies, and roasted meats. Ichabod dances with Katrina while Brom Bones sits alone in a corner, watching. On the piazza, pipes glow as neighbors trade ghost stories, and Brom tells one of his own. What did Ichabod carry with him when he left this party?
scenes.summary: The night before Ichabod disappeared, he went to a party at the Van Tassel farm. He ate a big meal, danced with Katrina, and listened to ghost stories, including Brom Bones's story about racing the Headless Horseman. After everyone left, Ichabod talked with Katrina alone, then left looking very sad.

scenes.narration: It is past midnight, and you follow the road Ichabod took home. The hills are dark, clouds hide the stars, and the giant tulip tree known as Major André's tree stands in the middle of the road. Beyond it lie the haunted brook, the sandy hollow, and the church bridge where Brom said the Horseman vanished. What did Ichabod see on this road, and what did he only fear?
scenes.summary: Ichabod rode home alone in the dark. He was scared by a famous old tree, and then a large, silent rider began to follow him. The rider seemed to have no head. Ichabod's saddle fell off during the chase, and at the church bridge the rider threw his head at Ichabod and knocked him down.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly moonless night on a wooded country road in the 1790s Hudson Valley, deep blues and blacks with faint silver starlight, eerie but not gory, no detailed faces, no readable text. Keep the upper-left area (the left two-fifths of the image, top third) as plain, empty, dark cloudy sky, because narration text overlays it. Upper right (x 62 to 92 percent, y 4 to 34 percent): an enormous gnarled tulip tree with twisting limbs, a pale lightning-scarred patch of bare white wood on its trunk. Center (x 40 to 62 percent, y 40 to 68 percent): a huge cloaked rider on a powerful black horse, a dark silhouette whose shoulders end with no visible head, a rounded dark shape resting on the saddle pommel in front of him. Lower-left foreground (x 6 to 30 percent, y 70 to 90 percent): an old leather saddle lying in the dusty road with a broken girth strap, deep hoofprints pressed around it. Lower right (x 66 to 94 percent, y 66 to 90 percent): a wooden plank bridge over a black brook that reflects one silver star, with the faint pale wall of a small whitewashed church on a knoll behind it. The tree and its white scar, the headless rider, the saddle, and the bridge must all be clearly visible.

scenes.narration: Years have passed, and Ichabod has never come back to Sleepy Hollow. The old wives still tell his story by the winter fire, a farmer has brought strange news from New York, and Brom Bones laughs whenever someone mentions the pumpkin. Even the man who first told this legend admits he has his doubts. Which version will your account trust?
scenes.summary: After Ichabod disappeared, people explained it in different ways. Many old women said a ghost took him. A farmer said Ichabod was alive in New York. Brom Bones married Katrina and laughed whenever people mentioned the pumpkin. The man who told the story said he did not believe half of it.
scenes.art_direction: Painterly, cozy winter evening inside an old Dutch farmhouse in the Hudson Valley, years later, warm orange firelight against cool blue window light, no detailed faces, no readable text. Keep the upper-left area (the left two-fifths of the image, top third) as plain, empty, dark ceiling beams in deep shadow, because narration text overlays it. Center-right (x 56 to 84 percent, y 30 to 60 percent): a wide stone hearth with a crackling fire where two elderly women in close caps sit at spinning wheels, leaning toward each other as if telling a tale. Lower-left foreground (x 4 to 28 percent, y 64 to 92 percent): a traveler's bundle, a walking stick, and a dusty hat resting by the door, as if a farmer has come home from a long journey. Lower center (x 34 to 58 percent, y 66 to 92 percent): a wooden table with a round orange pumpkin on it, and beside it a broad-shouldered man in a fur cap, seen from behind, shoulders shaking with laughter. Lower right (x 70 to 92 percent, y 68 to 92 percent): a small side table holding a half-filled wine glass, with a pepper-and-salt colored coat draped over a chair. Through a frosted window at the upper right, a tiny ruined schoolhouse is faintly visible in the snowy distance. The hearth with the storytellers, the traveler's bundle, the pumpkin with the laughing man, and the wine glass must all be clearly visible.

storybook.art_style:
One style for every page: a painterly storybook illustration in warm gouache on cream paper, with soft edges and visible brush texture. Gently comic in daylight, shadowy and eerie at night, never gory.
Palette: autumn golds, russet, and moss green by day; deep blue-black, gray mist, and pale moonlight by night, with lantern amber as the warm accent.
Setting: a quiet Dutch farming valley near the Hudson River, about 1790: rolling wooded hills, a brook, split-rail fences, a log schoolhouse, stone farmhouses with low sloping roofs, a small church and its wooden bridge.
Ichabod Crane: very tall and thin, narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, big hands and feet, a small head with large ears, large green glassy eyes, and a long pointed nose; loose, rusty-black clothes. Drawn with affection, like a storybook scarecrow, never mocked cruelly.
The Headless Horseman: only ever a dark cloaked rider on a huge black horse, seen from a distance or in silhouette, with no head and nothing shown at the neck. Never a wound.
Never: words, letters, or numbers in the image; blood or injury; caricatured faces; anything a later page reveals.

characters_met.name: Diedrich Knickerbocker
characters_met.description: A man, now dead, among whose papers this story was found.

characters_met.name: The narrator
characters_met.description: The person telling the story, who says he only repeats what he was told.

restatements.5f99c22b30c61d5e: This story was found among the papers of Diedrich Knickerbocker, who has died.
restatements.55dfe1e80ad4bf2c: These lines of poetry describe a sleepy, pleasant land full of daydreams.
restatements.3f72bc7c482665ab: The lines come from a poem called The Castle of Indolence. Indolence means laziness.
restatements.b649aa99405f3c72: On the east shore of the Hudson River, at a wide part the old Dutch sailors called the Tappan Zee, there is a small market town. Some call it Greensburgh, but most call it Tarry Town.
restatements.c9a1790abc691a9d: People say the name came from local wives, because their husbands liked to linger at the village tavern on market days.
restatements.a2f803caabc9779f: I can't say if this is true, but I mention it to be accurate.
restatements.d98c0d0f9760f831: About two miles from the village, there's a very quiet valley among hills.
restatements.acffa76a5b4a716c: A small brook runs through it with a soft, sleepy sound. A quail's whistle or a woodpecker's tapping is almost the only noise that breaks the quiet.

illustration.alt: A small quiet valley among high hills near a wide river, with a brook running through it.
illustration.scene_description: Wide view, late afternoon. The broad, calm Hudson River (the Tappan Zee) with a small river town on its shore in the distance. In the foreground, a little valley tucked among high wooded hills, with a small brook winding through it. A quail on a fence rail and a woodpecker on a tree trunk. Quiet and sleepy, with no people in close view.

bridge.summary: The storyteller remembers hunting squirrels in this valley when he was a boy; the roar of his own gun startled him because the place was so quiet. The valley is called Sleepy Hollow, and the families who live there come from the first Dutch settlers. Some say the place is under a spell. Its people believe in marvels, see strange sights, and hear music and voices in the air, and the valley is full of local tales, haunted places, and superstitions.

characters_met.name: The Headless Horseman
characters_met.description: A ghost rider with no head. Some say he is a Hessian soldier from the Revolutionary War who rides at night looking for his head.

restatements.bbe3cacaed94e764: The main ghost in this magical area is a headless figure on a horse.
restatements.eda282142fdc064a: Some people say it's the ghost of a Hessian soldier who lost his head in a war.
restatements.069ba6cc326c734b: He is seen not just in the valley but also on nearby roads, especially near a church.
restatements.9605082d995d7d96: Some historians say the ghost rides at night looking for his head and rushes back to the churchyard before morning.
restatements.d4958eaf3bdbaef3: This legend has inspired many stories, and the ghost is called the Headless Horseman of Sleepy Hollow.

illustration.alt: In the dark, a headless rider on a horse races along a road near a distant church.
illustration.scene_description: Night, seen from far away. A dark rider in a long cloak on a galloping horse, shown only in silhouette against a misty, moonlit sky, racing along a country road like a gust of wind. The rider has no head; nothing is shown at the neck. A small church on a rise in the distance. Dark, windy, and mysterious, not gory.

bridge.summary: Even people who move to the valley start to daydream and see ghosts after living there a while. The storyteller explains that small, quiet Dutch valleys like this one stay the same while the rest of the country keeps changing. He thinks that if he went back today, he would find the same trees and the same families there.

characters_met.name: Ichabod Crane
characters_met.description: The schoolteacher of Sleepy Hollow, from Connecticut: very tall and thin, with big ears, big green eyes, and a long nose.

restatements.102a23aa5135f236: In this quiet place, about thirty years ago, lived a man named Ichabod Crane. He stayed in Sleepy Hollow to teach the local children.
restatements.e0a54c107b747580: He was from Connecticut, a state known for sending out many teachers and pioneers.
restatements.4216e98d9482d1f6: The last name Crane suited him well.
restatements.9dfd964b052d1116: He was very tall and thin, with narrow shoulders, long arms and legs, and big hands and feet.
restatements.8bb49ea9d2652fab: His head was small and flat on top, with big ears, large green eyes, and a long nose.
restatements.3419ce6c320cd379: When he walked on a windy day, he looked like a scarecrow or a spirit of hunger.

illustration.alt: A tall, thin schoolmaster with big ears and a long nose strides along a windy hilltop, his clothes flapping.
illustration.scene_description: Daytime, windy. Ichabod Crane striding along the top of a hill, seen in profile against the sky. He is tall and very thin, with long arms and legs, big hands dangling out of his sleeves, big feet, a small head with huge ears, large green eyes, and a long pointed nose. His loose clothes flap and balloon in the wind, so he looks a little like a scarecrow. Gently funny.

restatements.138aee8e3e40a03c: His schoolhouse was a small, simple building made of logs. The windows had some glass and some old paper patches.
restatements.78d6931928865b05: It was cleverly locked with a twisted stick and stakes on the windows. This made it easy to get in but hard to get out, like an eel trap.
restatements.a418dccba49531a7: The schoolhouse was in a quiet but nice spot by a hill, with a brook nearby and a big birch tree at one end.
restatements.a664e336e45f6e8c: On a sleepy summer day, you could hear the students quietly studying, like bees buzzing. Sometimes, the teacher's strict voice or the sound of a birch stick would interrupt.
restatements.2fca7cf00e5d3aec: He was a careful teacher and believed in the saying, 'Spare the rod and spoil the child.'
restatements.12af6e3f5d3b0ee8: Ichabod Crane's students were definitely not spoiled.

illustration.alt: A one-room log schoolhouse at the foot of a wooded hill, beside a brook and a birch tree.
illustration.scene_description: A drowsy summer day. A low, one-room schoolhouse built roughly of logs, at the foot of a wooded hill, with a brook running close by and a large birch tree growing at one end. Some windows have glass; others are patched with pages from old copybooks. LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE: the door's twisted-branch fastening and the stakes set against the window shutters.
illustration.missing_detail: How the schoolhouse is locked when no one is there: a withe (twisted branch) in the door handle and stakes set against the window shutters ("a withe twisted in the handle of the door, and stakes set against the window shutters").

bridge.summary: Ichabod is not a cruel teacher, but he does punish students with a birch rod, mostly the tough ones, and tells them they will thank him for it someday. He earns very little, so he lives with his students' families, a week at a time, carrying everything he owns tied up in a cotton handkerchief. He eats an enormous amount. To stay welcome, he helps with farm chores and pets the youngest children. He also teaches singing and is proud of his loud voice in church. The women of the valley admire him as an educated man, and he carries gossip from house to house. He has read Cotton Mather's book about witchcraft in New England, and he firmly believes every word of it.

restatements.061207c948a90ede: He was a mix of being a little clever and very gullible.
restatements.7c8a6be50cfe4f4f: He loved strange stories and believed them easily, especially after living in this magical place.
restatements.c790fd95c723fc34: No story was too wild for him to believe.
restatements.7c43e6c675a3fab4: After school, he liked to lie on the grass and read scary stories until it got too dark.
restatements.64f1c474c5d31f21: As he walked home through the woods, every sound made his imagination run wild.
restatements.d34e73629f2488be: Fireflies and beetles sometimes scared him, making him think of witches.
restatements.11e4a1c088bb2114: To calm himself, he sang psalm tunes, and people in Sleepy Hollow could hear his voice from far away.

illustration.alt: At dusk, Ichabod lies on clover by a brook, reading a book, as fireflies begin to glow.
illustration.scene_description: Evening. Ichabod stretched out on a thick bed of clover beside the little brook near his schoolhouse, reading an old book of witch tales, holding it close because the light is fading. Woods and swamp darken behind him. LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE: the fireflies sparkling in the darkest places.
illustration.missing_detail: Fireflies sparkling in the darkest places ("The fireflies, too, which sparkled most vividly in the darkest places").

restatements.db71b7b8d89f1fdf: Ichabod Crane liked to spend winter nights with old Dutch women, listening to their ghost stories, especially about the Headless Horseman.
restatements.5bf3a8c16889978e: He entertained them with stories about witchcraft and scary things from Connecticut, and even frightened them with tales about comets and the world spinning.
restatements.bd69a6b9916247af: While he enjoyed these stories by the warm fire, he paid for it with fear on his walk home.
restatements.3f90e6428b950a40: Scary shapes and shadows appeared on his path during snowy nights.
restatements.39bdf8c8fc3f39a8: He looked hopefully at every light coming from faraway windows.
restatements.d96b54250433d86a: He was often scared by snow-covered bushes that looked like ghosts.
restatements.6a06be8a618a1c1b: He was frightened by the sound of his own footsteps and worried something was behind him.
restatements.7224c0f5992f647d: He was terrified by the wind in the trees, thinking it was the Headless Horseman.
restatements.049c9768b5c126f0: These were just nighttime fears. Daylight made them disappear, and he would have been happy if not for a woman who caused him more trouble than ghosts.

illustration.alt: On a snowy night, Ichabod walks home alone across dark fields, glancing over his shoulder.
illustration.scene_description: A snowy winter night. Ichabod walking home alone along a path across empty, snow-covered fields, looking nervously over his shoulder. A snow-covered shrub beside the path looks a little like a ghost in a sheet. Bare trees bend in the wind. LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE: the trembling ray of light from a distant window across the fields.
illustration.missing_detail: A trembling ray of light streaming across the fields from a distant window ("every trembling ray of light streaming across the waste fields from some distant window").

characters_met.name: Katrina Van Tassel
characters_met.description: The 18-year-old only child of a rich Dutch farmer. She takes Ichabod's singing lessons and is famous for her beauty and the fortune she will inherit.

restatements.0f77c1790567eab2: Katrina Van Tassel, the daughter of a wealthy Dutch farmer, was one of the students who came each week for singing lessons.
restatements.828919b9c69a46f4: She was a pretty 18-year-old girl, as lovely as her father's peaches, and known for her beauty and wealth.
restatements.e721026b882ac317: She was a bit of a flirt, which showed in her clothes that mixed old and new styles to highlight her looks.
restatements.43b464766489dad8: She wore gold jewelry from her great-great-grandmother and a short skirt to show off her pretty feet and ankles.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture Katrina Van Tassel as the story describes her. Describe her dress and her gold ornaments.

characters_met.name: Baltus Van Tassel
characters_met.description: Katrina's father, a cheerful, generous farmer with a rich farm on the Hudson.

restatements.60590e5cdba960fa: Ichabod Crane was easily charmed by women, and he liked Katrina Van Tassel after visiting her home.
restatements.4656af847308837a: Old Baltus Van Tassel was a happy and generous farmer who was doing well.
restatements.e4fe222b09072eb1: He rarely thought about anything outside his farm, but everything there was nice and well-kept.
restatements.7bed6c4195bea12f: He was happy with his wealth and liked having plenty, not showing off.
restatements.71c5b031447c5203: His home was by the Hudson River in a green, cozy spot where Dutch farmers liked to live.
restatements.701b046b8a65e726: A big elm tree shaded a spring of fresh water that flowed into a nearby brook.
restatements.96ce15fac89d45ff: Near the farmhouse was a huge barn full of farm goods, with birds flying around it.
restatements.aee6d80a5201583f: Fat pigs rested in their pens, and baby pigs sometimes came out to sniff the air.
restatements.9bf673575f136791: Geese swam in a pond with ducks, and turkeys and Guinea fowls made noise in the yard.
restatements.e0c81146ec84fa8c: A proud rooster crowed and called his family to eat the food he found.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the Van Tassel farm. Describe the elm tree and the spring, the huge barn, and the animals in the farmyard.

restatements.e01dc6336d8b03b9: The teacher's mouth watered as he thought about the delicious winter food.
restatements.da03c52b0f3118ff: In his mind, he imagined pigs with pudding and apples, pigeons in pies, and geese in gravy.
restatements.38be9c2d185ed683: He saw pork becoming bacon and ham, turkeys with sausages, and even the rooster cooked and ready to eat.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture what Ichabod imagines as he looks at the farm animals. Describe the funniest dish he dreams up.

bridge.summary: Ichabod looks over Van Tassel's rich fields and orchards and daydreams about marrying Katrina, selling the land, and heading west with her and a wagon full of children. Inside, the farmhouse is full of treasures: shining pewter, strings of dried fruit and corn on the walls, polished furniture, and old silver. From that moment, Ichabod thinks only about winning Katrina. It will not be easy. She keeps changing her mind, and she has many other admirers, who watch each other jealously and gang up on any newcomer.

characters_met.name: Brom Bones
characters_met.description: Abraham "Brom" Van Brunt: a big, strong, bold rider who leads a gang of friends and loves pranks more than fights.

restatements.c485d134a7149876: The toughest of them was a big, loud guy named Abraham, or Brom Van Brunt, known for his strength and bravery.
restatements.5a458f618f381f79: He was strong and had curly black hair, with a face that looked both fun and proud.
restatements.a21f6f2ec0db4ae1: Because of his strong body, he was called Brom Bones by everyone.
restatements.f4d9908aee32153c: He was very skilled at riding horses, as good as a Tartar.
restatements.73663a7cb75a06a9: He led in races and cockfights, and his strength made him the judge in arguments, deciding without question.
restatements.b9dadbfae17d7832: He was always up for a fight or fun, but he was more playful than mean.
restatements.9dbfb106215a1ea1: He had a few close friends who looked up to him, and they traveled around causing trouble or having fun.
restatements.94e1c075010985b5: In winter, he wore a fur cap with a fox's tail, and people knew trouble was coming when they saw it.
restatements.cb8bd9f80b1cf879: Sometimes, he and his friends would ride noisily past houses at night, and people would say, 'There goes Brom Bones and his gang!'
restatements.49777b184f253f5c: People felt a mix of fear, admiration, and liking for him, and blamed him for any wild pranks or fights.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture Brom Bones as the story describes him. Describe his size, his fur cap with the fox tail, and his gang of riders.

bridge.summary: Brom has been courting Katrina for some time, and people whisper that she does not entirely discourage him. When his horse is tied outside the Van Tassel house on a Sunday night, other young men stay away. Ichabod is no match for Brom's strength, but he is like a bendable stick: he bends but never breaks. He courts Katrina quietly, visiting the farmhouse as her singing teacher, and her easygoing parents let her do as she likes. Once Ichabod starts visiting, Brom's horse stops appearing on Sunday nights, and a bitter feud grows between Brom and the schoolmaster.

restatements.18ff597d6596edab: Brom wanted to fight Ichabod for Katrina, like knights did long ago. But Ichabod knew Brom was stronger and avoided a fight.
restatements.6b221f88bd09e892: Ichabod's peaceful way of avoiding fights annoyed Brom, so he played mean jokes on him instead.
restatements.8b1474990b9dd1a0: Ichabod became the target of Brom's silly tricks and jokes.
restatements.5ce334cd0a033f16: Brom and his friends messed up Ichabod's school and singing class, making him think witches were involved.
restatements.6b49bd26b0789fa9: Brom embarrassed Ichabod in front of Katrina by teaching a dog to whine like Ichabod singing.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture one of Brom's pranks on Ichabod. Describe the schoolhouse or the singing school when it happens.

bridge.summary: One autumn afternoon, while Ichabod watches over his quiet schoolroom, a messenger on a half-wild colt gallops up to the door. He brings an invitation to a party at the Van Tassels' house that evening. Ichabod rushes the students through their lessons and lets them out an hour early, and the children burst outside, shouting with joy.

pages.content_note: The next part of Irving's original text includes racist caricatures of Black people that were common in writing of the 1820s. They are wrong and hurtful. Your teacher or parent may read and discuss this part with you.

characters_met.name: Hans Van Ripper
characters_met.description: A hot-tempered old Dutch farmer. Ichabod lives at his house and borrows his old horse, Gunpowder.

restatements.7c977a19f243227d: Ichabod spent extra time getting ready, fixing his only black suit and hair.
restatements.d20608278a121fe5: He borrowed a horse from Hans Van Ripper to impress his lady like a knight.
restatements.ec0ce68dcb8265f1: I should describe how Ichabod and his horse looked.
restatements.ae3a132d8bba285c: The horse was an old plow-horse, still mean despite its age.
restatements.4f9e846e22b5e102: It was thin, with a bent neck and tangled mane, and had one scary eye.
restatements.6fc7d2f1e225c059: The horse was once spirited, as its name, Gunpowder, suggests.
restatements.2ed24e134a5032fb: Hans Van Ripper, a fierce rider, likely passed some of his spirit to the horse.
restatements.be2ca7d5dc5b7e4e: Ichabod looked like he belonged on such a horse.
restatements.ecadf5db7705f59f: He rode with short stirrups, elbows out, and his arms flapped like wings.
restatements.08a912a6b80abd1c: His small hat sat on his nose, and his coat tails fluttered behind.
restatements.0ae7f5c9de0cf7d4: Ichabod and his horse looked unusual as they left Hans Van Ripper's gate.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture Ichabod setting out on Gunpowder. Describe the horse, Ichabod's clothes, and how he sits in the saddle.

bridge.summary: It is a beautiful autumn day. The forests are brown and yellow, some trees are orange, purple, and scarlet, and birds flutter everywhere. As Ichabod rides, he looks at the apples, corn, pumpkins, and buckwheat and imagines the pies, cakes, and pancakes they will become, served to him by Katrina. The sun sets over the wide, still Hudson River as he rides along the hills.

restatements.988cfde313157955: In the evening, Ichabod arrived at Van Tassel's house, which was full of important local people.
restatements.1a8d62dcd87fa5d2: There were old farmers with thin, leathery faces, wearing homemade clothes and big shoes with shiny buckles.
restatements.67312abf2daf942c: Their lively, small wives wore caps, long dresses, and had colorful pockets outside their skirts.
restatements.ff623f9db8d52178: Young women, almost as old-fashioned as their mothers, wore hats, ribbons, or white dresses showing city style.
restatements.ce4169b2f8cd75e1: The sons wore short coats with big buttons and often tied their hair with eel-skin, thought to make hair strong.
restatements.63c5dc4e48efa817: Brom Bones was the star of the event, arriving on his wild horse Daredevil, which only he could control.
restatements.d559e110d2b5ca17: He liked wild horses that did tricks and were risky to ride, thinking tame horses were boring.

restatements.6bb3dadb000db9c5: I wish I could stop to describe the amazing sights Ichabod saw when he entered Van Tassel's fancy room.
restatements.4a0ca285c0ddaad5: It wasn't the pretty girls, but the wonderful Dutch tea-table full of autumn treats.
restatements.3bdd16b860fe010b: There were piles of cakes of many kinds, only known to skilled Dutch housewives!
restatements.02c3e66dd708b5b7: There were doughnuts, soft oly koek, crunchy crullers, sweet cakes, and honey cakes.
restatements.832dbaab7cb3a3c8: There were also apple, peach, and pumpkin pies, ham, smoked beef, preserved fruits, broiled fish, roasted chickens, and bowls of milk and cream, all mixed together with a steaming teapot in the middle.
restatements.b7a314a88495595b: I don't have enough time to describe this feast properly, and I'm eager to continue the story.
restatements.1aecb63e369d117e: Luckily, Ichabod Crane took his time and enjoyed every delicious treat.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the tea table at the Van Tassels' party. Describe the cakes, pies, and other food as the story does.

restatements.9325ff64d6b4bbf8: He was happy and grateful, feeling better as he ate more, like some people do when they drink.
restatements.f13bba4fe778f6f2: He imagined himself owning all this luxury and laughed at the thought.
restatements.01897307f36206f5: He thought about how quickly he would leave the old schoolhouse, snap his fingers at Hans Van Ripper and the other stingy people he had boarded with, and kick out any traveling teacher who called him a friend.
restatements.53a9d061d7fb27c2: Old Baltus Van Tassel was cheerful and happy, like a big, round harvest moon.
restatements.4b02fc93534882a8: He greeted guests with a handshake, a shoulder pat, a laugh, and told them to enjoy the food.

characters_met.name: The fiddler
characters_met.description: An old, gray-haired musician who has played for the neighborhood's dances for more than fifty years.

restatements.4927a12d01e4984f: The music from the main room called everyone to start dancing.
restatements.d8b21d243e15db98: The musician was an old gray-haired man who had been playing music in the area for over fifty years.
restatements.ebddffbb47ca7824: His instrument was as old and worn out as he was.
restatements.78b847290e3b979e: Most of the time, he played on just a few strings, moving his head with the music and stomping his foot when a new couple began dancing.
restatements.79ee3ca0acd8849b: Ichabod was as proud of his dancing as he was of his singing.
restatements.fbdbf48be4b0d1a5: Every part of his loose, lanky body moved as he clattered around the room, as if the saint of dancing himself were dancing.
restatements.4e00fa1fd2ad8363: Black people of all ages from the farm and the neighborhood crowded at every door and window, watching Ichabod dance with delight. (The original sentence describes them with an insulting stereotype.)
restatements.037035b392a0013a: How could Ichabod, who disciplined children, not be happy and excited?
restatements.aa96fbea4aac6898: The girl he liked was his dance partner, smiling at him, while Brom Bones sat alone, feeling jealous.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture Ichabod dancing with Katrina while Brom sits in the corner. Describe how each of them moves or sits.
pages.content_note: The next part of Irving's original text includes racist caricatures of Black people that were common in writing of the 1820s. They are wrong and hurtful. Your teacher or parent may read and discuss this part with you.

bridge.summary: After the dance, Ichabod joins the older men who sit smoking on the porch with old Van Tassel. They tell long stories about the Revolutionary War, which was fought near this neighborhood. Each storyteller has made his own part bigger over the years, and each one believes he helped win the war.

characters_met.name: Major André
characters_met.description: A British officer from the Revolutionary War who was captured near a great tree in the neighborhood.

restatements.bf29e0cbe5d8ad6b: The ghost stories that followed were even more amazing.
restatements.5096ddc3c633661a: This area is full of legendary stories.
restatements.05e4e3a29d4d8f1e: Old tales and superstitions do well in these quiet, settled places.
restatements.3e168c8fe840e25a: Ghosts don't appear much in villages because people move away quickly.
restatements.bd15501470d26a42: That's why we mostly hear ghost stories in old Dutch communities.
restatements.7ef1a757a9764fb0: The many ghost stories here are because of Sleepy Hollow nearby.
restatements.13313e7b5a293a1e: The air from Sleepy Hollow spreads dreams and fantasies everywhere.
restatements.14b1738c27519d87: Some people from Sleepy Hollow were at Van Tassel's, sharing their stories.
restatements.d3be6cd4c7a7433f: They told sad stories about cries and wails near the tree where Major André was captured.
restatements.e990309d9fdbafca: They also talked about a woman in white who haunts Raven Rock and screams before storms.
restatements.f020e3d794bbe602: Most stories were about the Headless Horseman, who is said to tie his horse by the graves.

characters_met.name: Old Brouwer
characters_met.description: A man in one of the ghost stories who did not believe in ghosts until he met the Headless Horseman.

restatements.f997ff321f15d6ea: The church's hidden location makes it a favorite spot for ghosts.
restatements.7ea3acab72e0fa02: It sits on a small hill, surrounded by trees, with its white walls shining like purity.
restatements.b1e926b01332217c: A gentle slope leads to a shiny water area, with views of the Hudson hills.
restatements.7bc395328f3bf863: The churchyard is so peaceful that it seems like the dead could rest quietly there.
restatements.92908a1380c6f4cd: Next to the church is a wide wooded area with a large brook flowing through rocks and fallen trees.
restatements.fc83f37d554113b9: A wooden bridge used to cross a dark part of the stream, shaded by trees, making it very dark at night.
restatements.982c75dd56a5a694: This was a favorite spot of the Headless Horseman, where he was often seen.
restatements.067a89937b921d10: A story tells of old Brouwer, who didn't believe in ghosts, meeting the Horseman and being thrown into a brook.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the old church and its bridge as the story describes them. Describe the light, the trees, and the sounds.

restatements.67a6e5b529c84e27: Brom Bones shared an amazing story about the Galloping Hessian, treating him like just a regular rider.
restatements.0efedf8548605cbd: He said that one night, after leaving Sing Sing, he raced the ghostly rider for a bowl of punch. Daredevil, his horse, was winning until the Hessian disappeared in a flash of fire at the church bridge.
restatements.e61d96ad9bac829c: These stories, told in a sleepy voice, made a big impression on Ichabod as he listened.
restatements.3768f0dbb72eadb5: Ichabod shared stories from his favorite author, Cotton Mather, and talked about strange things he saw in Connecticut and Sleepy Hollow.

restatements.8805143c823398b1: The party slowly came to an end.
restatements.946cf4be23efee0d: The farmers gathered their families into wagons and drove away on the roads.
restatements.56c8b855c3e1ae64: Some girls rode behind their favorite boys, laughing as they went, until the sounds faded away.
restatements.169bf3ad01e4ed67: Ichabod stayed behind to talk privately with the heiress, thinking he was close to winning her over.
restatements.4baa084abe028bc3: I don't know what happened during their talk.
restatements.8483faba3bae5437: Something must have gone wrong because Ichabod left looking sad and disappointed.
restatements.3abbe78e8ca19bea: Was the girl just playing tricks on him?
restatements.5a4f4c53c460a03c: Was she pretending to like him to win over his rival?
restatements.30a097e5524fe44e: Ichabod left looking like he had stolen chickens instead of winning a girl's heart.
restatements.e8ffc33aa3558c55: He didn't look around at the farm he admired before, and he rudely woke up his horse.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the end of the party. Describe the farmhouse, the people leaving, and the night outside.

restatements.249c6035b6663764: It was late at night when Ichabod, feeling sad and down, headed home along the hills above Tarry Town, which he had happily crossed earlier.
restatements.dea57eb9525327d3: The time of night was as gloomy as he felt.
restatements.7d5d4d1a04a9c9a1: Below him, the Tappan Zee looked dark and unclear, with a few ship masts quietly anchored near the shore.
restatements.1b9cc3ab14a2db17: In the quiet of midnight, he could faintly hear a dog barking from across the Hudson River, showing how far away it was.
restatements.b328602c87b35e4b: Sometimes, a rooster would crow far away from a farmhouse in the hills, sounding like a distant dream.
restatements.bef74a5c5648bf3e: There were no signs of life nearby, except for the sad chirp of a cricket or the sound of a bullfrog in a marsh.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture Ichabod riding home alone at midnight. Describe the hills, the river, and the sounds in the dark.

restatements.d683d688103ba639: All the ghost stories he heard earlier came back to his mind.
restatements.8b50fb8cdab70a45: The night got darker, and clouds sometimes hid the stars.
restatements.0b0b7af7dec429b4: He felt very lonely and sad.
restatements.28bc977532fdbea0: He was getting close to where many ghost stories happened.
restatements.374a7eb513ae49d7: A huge tulip-tree stood in the middle of the road, taller than other trees.
restatements.889bfdd4815183be: Its branches were twisted and big enough to be tree trunks.
restatements.500ad81796a533f3: The tree was linked to the sad story of André, who was captured nearby.
restatements.afa4347bd60546e9: People respected and feared the tree because of André's fate and spooky tales.

restatements.97cbdb0e201c5b4c: As Ichabod got closer to the scary tree, he started to whistle and thought he heard a reply, but it was just the wind blowing through the branches.
restatements.5b78552caa56cc8b: When he got nearer, he thought he saw something white in the tree. He stopped whistling and realized it was just a spot where lightning had hit the tree.
restatements.e95b57c0ec54dc55: Suddenly, he heard a groan, which made his teeth chatter and knees shake. It was just branches rubbing together in the wind.
restatements.d623b3dfc36c5861: He safely passed the tree, but more dangers awaited him.
restatements.85412e6078a1b6b5: About two hundred yards from the tree, a small brook crossed the road and led into a swampy, wooded area called Wiley’s Swamp.
restatements.7445d6c8c70f083d: A few rough logs made a bridge over this stream.
restatements.3c6e463f6e2fd5de: On the side where the brook entered the woods, thick grapevines covered the oaks and chestnuts, making it very dark.
restatements.d50435a7bf653cbb: Crossing this bridge was the hardest part.
restatements.b632a5bc4ec9cd10: This was the exact spot where André was captured, and where the men hid to surprise him.
restatements.aefe914f062ad1ff: Since then, the stream has been thought to be haunted, and schoolboys are scared to pass it alone at night.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the great tree and the little brook. Describe the shapes, the shadows, and the light.

restatements.e44b2603c39338b5: As he got closer to the stream, his heart started beating fast. He tried to cross the bridge quickly by kicking his horse, but the horse moved sideways and hit the fence.
restatements.b40884ea99a4adc1: Ichabod got more scared and pulled the reins, kicking the horse again. The horse just ran into some bushes on the other side of the road.
restatements.e8bce09bc2248c86: Ichabod used both his whip and heels on the horse, which ran forward but stopped suddenly at the bridge, almost throwing Ichabod off.
restatements.05d5bb36b0b18104: Just then, Ichabod heard a splashy sound near the bridge.
restatements.3f7f9f201bb4d349: In the dark shadows by the brook, he saw something big and strange.
restatements.035a4528216fe511: It didn't move but looked like a giant monster ready to jump at him.

restatements.f4f3f47462f56b76: The scared teacher's hair stood up in fear.
restatements.039da921b48f27a0: It was too late to run away, and how could he escape a ghost or goblin that could fly?
restatements.96f14dc48c19aba5: Trying to be brave, he asked nervously, 'Who are you?'
restatements.6455c1c68999dc1d: He asked again, even more nervously.
restatements.74ae9d74d62dce15: He hit Gunpowder's sides and started singing a psalm with his eyes closed.
restatements.231648ba2491620b: Then the scary shape moved and jumped into the middle of the road.
restatements.aff810614e3358ce: Even though it was dark, he could see the shape a little better.
restatements.270e17ec224b8162: It looked like a big horseman on a strong black horse.
restatements.b8fd35089b58e412: The horseman didn't bother him but stayed on the side of the road, riding next to Gunpowder.

restatements.8a26a24a7e9f00be: Ichabod didn't like this strange rider and remembered Brom Bones' story about the Galloping Hessian. He tried to ride faster to leave him behind.
restatements.3b58ab7f8682341d: The stranger also sped up his horse to match Ichabod's pace.
restatements.dd82cae5c4f6bb06: Ichabod slowed down to a walk, hoping the stranger would pass, but the stranger did the same.
restatements.c4f5b68f19cc3e8e: Ichabod felt scared and tried to sing a psalm, but his mouth was too dry to sing.
restatements.38d5a3af065a6e06: The silent and stubborn way the stranger followed was mysterious and scary.
restatements.9f66586fa539fed3: The reason for this fear soon became clear.
restatements.c2965a437703641b: When they reached a hill, Ichabod saw the stranger's silhouette against the sky and realized he had no head!
restatements.011510c39d566718: Ichabod was even more terrified when he saw the head was on the saddle in front of the stranger.
restatements.6cbaf96a8fd58caf: In a panic, Ichabod kicked and hit his horse to escape, but the ghostly rider kept up with him.
restatements.3924238537ade9ae: They raced through everything, with stones flying and sparks lighting up the night.
restatements.1440ac90b790b265: Ichabod's clothes flapped in the wind as he leaned forward over his horse, trying to get away.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the stranger riding beside Ichabod. Describe only what Ichabod can see in the dark.

restatements.c950b6c9df84ce64: They reached the road to Sleepy Hollow, but Gunpowder turned the wrong way and ran downhill.
restatements.54951700d86bcbca: This road goes through a sandy area with trees, crosses a famous bridge, and leads to a church.
restatements.78d1792394c9ca95: The horse's panic helped Ichabod in the chase, but then the saddle started to slip off.
restatements.025c12642b102d32: He tried to hold the saddle, but it fell off, and he clung to Gunpowder's neck.
restatements.115b659700d940f3: He worried about Hans Van Ripper's anger over the saddle, but the goblin was close behind.
restatements.5b2bafb5f3b282e0: He struggled to stay on the horse, slipping and bouncing painfully.

restatements.1cc706af69ba278c: Ichabod saw an opening in the trees and hoped the church bridge was near.
restatements.18c20505d72598f9: The reflection of a star in the brook showed he was right.
restatements.18871a482f6bbe84: He saw the church walls dimly through the trees.
restatements.76482a1fcdf51751: He remembered where Brom Bones's ghostly rival had vanished.
restatements.cfdf00e0141c52ce: Ichabod thought, 'If I can reach that bridge, I'll be safe.'
restatements.ce8f1cc4d89861c8: He heard the black horse breathing heavily behind him and thought he felt its breath.
restatements.9d19ee44d5ac8dce: Ichabod kicked his horse, Gunpowder, who ran onto the bridge and crossed it. Ichabod looked back to see if the ghost would disappear.
restatements.48de6e752b2bb4d3: He saw the ghost rise in the saddle and throw its head at him.
restatements.2bb12535e0323e65: Ichabod tried to dodge the head, but he was too late.
restatements.290a42792a44e52a: The head hit him hard, knocking him off his horse. Gunpowder, the black horse, and the ghost rider sped past like a whirlwind.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the church bridge at the moment Ichabod reaches it. Describe the bridge, the light, and the motion.

restatements.062ec0813364517f: The next morning, the old horse was found without its saddle, calmly eating grass at its owner's gate.
restatements.1457d171f9f890db: Ichabod didn't show up for breakfast or dinner.
restatements.81b0c5bc8a336b62: The boys gathered at the schoolhouse and wandered by the brook, but the schoolmaster was missing.
restatements.a9b9b1cc1b9d18fd: Hans Van Ripper started to worry about what happened to Ichabod and his saddle.
restatements.849de11bd8226ea6: They started looking for him and soon found some clues.
restatements.d6397b6e2fd8a119: On the road to the church, they found the saddle in the dirt and horse tracks leading to the bridge. Near the brook, they found Ichabod's hat and a broken pumpkin.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the brook near the church bridge the next morning. Describe what the searchers find.

restatements.f195474996cafe73: They searched the brook, but they couldn't find the schoolmaster's body.
restatements.b92fa82e8e48dd84: Hans Van Ripper, as the person in charge of Ichabod's belongings, looked through his things.
restatements.72e0ba2af1251367: Ichabod's belongings included some shirts, neckwear, stockings, old pants, a razor, a psalm book, and a broken pitch-pipe.
restatements.eb66dcec9889a92f: The schoolhouse books and furniture belonged to the town, except Cotton Mather's History of Witchcraft, an almanac, and a book of dreams and fortune-telling. In that last book was a sheet of paper full of scribbled, crossed-out tries at writing a poem for the Van Tassel heiress.
restatements.750f91825fc98d7a: Hans Van Ripper burned the personal books and paper, deciding not to send his kids to school anymore, thinking reading and writing were useless.
restatements.38a9462ee792a1d4: Ichabod had his money with him when he disappeared, as he had just been paid.

restatements.0b02630e95fe8c73: The strange event made people talk a lot at the church on Sunday.
restatements.1e6374c9fc7f7b48: Groups of people gathered at the churchyard, bridge, and where the hat and pumpkin were found.
restatements.745ee2bb2ae7ebb4: They remembered stories about Brouwer, Bones, and others, and decided Ichabod was taken by the Galloping Hessian.
restatements.d7bfdb8ee369fcf8: Since Ichabod was single and owed no one, nobody worried about him. The school moved, and a new teacher took over.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the people talking at the church on Sunday. Describe the scene by the bridge.

restatements.94ab9b3ef6f12667: An old farmer who visited New York years later brought home news that Ichabod was still alive. He said Ichabod had left partly because he was afraid of the goblin and of Hans Van Ripper, and partly because Katrina had suddenly turned him down. He moved far away, taught school while studying law, became a lawyer and a politician, wrote for the newspapers, and finally became a judge in a small court. This farmer is also the person who told the story of the ghostly ride.
restatements.81e8f4ffc20a988b: Brom Bones married Katrina after Ichabod disappeared. He laughed whenever Ichabod's story was told, making people think he knew more than he said.

restatements.0b634dc2382b3219: The old country women say Ichabod was taken away by supernatural forces. They love telling this story by the fire in winter.
restatements.60fd5e3a481405bc: The bridge became very spooky, so the road was changed to go by the millpond instead.
restatements.5da9c03f0a4b6afc: The empty schoolhouse fell apart and is said to be haunted. People think they hear the teacher's sad singing in Sleepy Hollow.

restatements.e8f722b597a6808a: A note added at the end of the story.
restatements.7d9c64a66e120b6b: This note was found in Mr. Knickerbocker's own handwriting.
restatements.0f9b0aa9a46ca918: The story was told almost exactly as I heard it at a meeting in the old city of Manhattoes, with many important people there.
restatements.9fc88e860bd2e51b: The storyteller was a friendly, shabby old man in gray clothes, with a funny but sad face. I thought he might be poor because he tried hard to be entertaining.
restatements.476fd92367423916: When he finished the story, people laughed and clapped, especially some deputy aldermen who had been asleep most of the time.
restatements.5d541f0736f86329: But there was one tall, serious-looking old man with thick eyebrows who stayed serious, sometimes folding his arms and looking down, as if thinking.
restatements.e5e54da936c782f2: He was a careful man who only laughed when he had good reasons.
restatements.0681e5bba6ffcff9: When everyone stopped laughing and it was quiet, he leaned on his chair and asked what the story's lesson was and what it proved.
restatements.50c5a3a144e58dbc: The storyteller, about to drink some wine, paused, looked respectfully at the questioner, and said the story logically proved something.
restatements.3eb398a76e3b20bf: First, the storyteller says every situation in life has good sides, if we can take a joke.
restatements.de1c148341390692: Second, anyone who races against goblin riders will probably have a rough ride.
restatements.f0a6106d658e162f: So, he jokes, a country schoolteacher who gets turned down by a rich Dutch girl is sure to rise to an important job.

restatements.2c3451e0c7a6189d: The careful old man frowned even harder, confused by this reasoning, while the storyteller in gray looked at him as if he had won.
restatements.aeedde81b7a794c3: Finally, the old man said the story was interesting but a bit too unbelievable, and he had some doubts.
restatements.beef558c507867c5: The storyteller replied, "Honestly, sir, I don't believe half of it myself."
restatements.08a2572c0c6c790c: D. K. are the initials of Diedrich Knickerbocker.
restatements.ff45e4f357220205: This is the end of the story.

pages.frame_prompt: Picture the storyteller and the doubtful old gentleman. Describe how each of them looks and acts as the story ends.

accept.line:
He assisted the farmers
occasionally in the lighter labors of their farms, helped to make
hay, mended the fences, took the horses to water, drove the cows from
pasture, and cut wood for the winter fire.

In addition to his other vocations, he was the singing-master of the
neighborhood, and picked up many bright shillings by instructing the
young folks in psalmody.

Thus, by divers little makeshifts, in that ingenious way which is
commonly denominated “by hook and by crook,” the worthy pedagogue got on
tolerably enough, and was thought, by all who understood nothing of the
labor of headwork, to have a wonderfully easy life of it.

The revenue
arising from his school was small, and would have been scarcely
sufficient to furnish him with daily bread, for he was a huge feeder,
and, though lank, had the dilating powers of an anaconda; but to help
out his maintenance, he was, according to country custom in those
parts, boarded and lodged at the houses of the farmers whose children
he instructed.

accept.line:
Our man of letters, therefore, was peculiarly happy in the
smiles of all the country damsels.

The schoolmaster is generally a man of some importance in the female
circle of a rural neighborhood; being considered a kind of idle,
gentlemanlike personage, of vastly superior taste and accomplishments to
the rough country swains, and, indeed, inferior in learning only to the
parson.

He found favor in the eyes of the mothers by petting the children,
particularly the youngest; and like the lion bold, which whilom so
magnanimously the lamb did hold, he would sit with a child on one knee,
and rock a cradle with his foot for whole hours together.

His appearance, therefore, is apt to occasion some little stir
at the tea-table of a farmhouse, and the addition of a supernumerary
dish of cakes or sweetmeats, or, peradventure, the parade of a silver
teapot.

From his half-itinerant life, also, he was a kind of travelling gazette,
carrying the whole budget of local gossip from house to house, so that
his appearance was always greeted with satisfaction.

He was, moreover,
esteemed by the women as a man of great erudition, for he had read
several books quite through, and was a perfect master of Cotton Mather’s
“History of New England Witchcraft,” in which, by the way, he most
firmly and potently believed.

items.label: Sell the farm for cash and wild land

accept.line:
As the enraptured Ichabod fancied all this, and as he rolled his great
green eyes over the fat meadow lands, the rich fields of wheat, of rye,
of buckwheat, and Indian corn, and the orchards burdened with ruddy
fruit, which surrounded the warm tenement of Van Tassel, his heart
yearned after the damsel who was to inherit these domains, and his
imagination expanded with the idea, how they might be readily turned
into cash, and the money invested in immense tracts of wild land, and
shingle palaces in the wilderness.

items.label: Move west with Katrina and the children

accept.line:
Nay, his busy fancy already realized
his hopes, and presented to him the blooming Katrina, with a whole
family of children, mounted on the top of a wagon loaded with household
trumpery, with pots and kettles dangling beneath; and he beheld himself
bestriding a pacing mare, with a colt at her heels, setting out for
Kentucky, Tennessee,--or the Lord knows where!

items.label: Eat like a king all winter

accept.line:
The pedagogue’s mouth watered as he looked upon this sumptuous promise
of luxurious winter fare.

In his devouring mind’s eye, he pictured to
himself every roasting-pig running about with a pudding in his belly,
and an apple in his mouth; the pigeons were snugly put to bed in a
comfortable pie, and tucked in with a coverlet of crust; the geese were
swimming in their own gravy; and the ducks pairing cosily in dishes,
like snug married couples, with a decent competency of onion sauce.

In
the porkers he saw carved out the future sleek side of bacon, and juicy
relishing ham; not a turkey but he beheld daintily trussed up, with
its gizzard under its wing, and, peradventure, a necklace of savory
sausages; and even bright chanticleer himself lay sprawling on his back,
in a side dish, with uplifted claws, as if craving that quarter which
his chivalrous spirit disdained to ask while living.

items.label: Win the heiress, win the farm

accept.line:
From the moment Ichabod laid his eyes upon these regions of delight, the
peace of his mind was at an end, and his only study was how to gain the
affections of the peerless daughter of Van Tassel.

items.label: Turn his back on the schoolhouse

accept.line:
Then, he thought, how soon he’d turn his back upon the old
schoolhouse; snap his fingers in the face of Hans Van Ripper, and every
other niggardly patron, and kick any itinerant pedagogue out of doors
that should dare to call him comrade!

Among these, the most formidable was a burly, roaring, roystering blade,
of the name of Abraham, or, according to the Dutch abbreviation, Brom
Van Brunt, the hero of the country round, which rang with his feats of
strength and hardihood.

Such was the formidable rival with whom Ichabod Crane had to contend,
and, considering all things, a stouter man than he would have shrunk
from the competition, and a wiser man would have despaired.

Ichabod, on the contrary, had to win his way to
the heart of a country coquette, beset with a labyrinth of whims
and caprices, which were forever presenting new difficulties and
impediments; and he had to encounter a host of fearful adversaries of
real flesh and blood, the numerous rustic admirers, who beset every
portal to her heart, keeping a watchful and angry eye upon each other,
but ready to fly out in the common cause against any new competitor.

items.label: The rider appears by the bridge

accept.line:
In the dark shadow of the grove, on the margin
of the brook, he beheld something huge, misshapen and towering.

He
appeared to be a horseman of large dimensions, and mounted on a black
horse of powerful frame.

Just at this moment a plashy tramp by the side of the bridge caught the
sensitive ear of Ichabod.

Just then the shadowy object of
alarm put itself in motion, and with a scramble and a bound stood at
once in the middle of the road.

As yet the panic of the steed had given his unskilful rider an apparent
advantage in the chase, but just as he had got half way through the
hollow, the girths of the saddle gave way, and he felt it slipping from
under him.

He seized it by the pommel, and endeavored to hold it firm,
but in vain; and had just time to save himself by clasping old Gunpowder
round the neck, when the saddle fell to the earth, and he heard it
trampled under foot by his pursuer.

Another convulsive kick in the ribs, and
old Gunpowder sprang upon the bridge; he thundered over the resounding
planks; he gained the opposite side; and now Ichabod cast a look behind
to see if his pursuer should vanish, according to rule, in a flash of
fire and brimstone.

Just then he saw the goblin rising in his stirrups,
and in the very act of hurling his head at him.

It encountered his cranium
with a tremendous crash,--he was tumbled headlong into the dust, and
Gunpowder, the black steed, and the goblin rider, passed by like a
whirlwind.

other trees of the neighborhood, and formed a kind of landmark.

It was connected with the tragical story of the unfortunate

lightning.question: What hangs from the centre of the best parlor?
answer:
In one corner
stood a huge bag of wool, ready to be spun; in another, a quantity of
linsey-woolsey just from the loom; ears of Indian corn, and strings of
dried apples and peaches, hung in gay festoons along the walls, mingled

tongs, glistened from their covert of asparagus tops; mock-oranges and
conch-shells decorated the mantelpiece; strings of various-colored birds
eggs were suspended above it; a great ostrich egg was hung from
the centre of the room, and a corner cupboard, knowingly left open,
displayed immense treasures of old silver and well-mended china.

witnesses.caught: Hmph. They swear he was spirited away. And who am I to argue?

cards: Have you heard news of the schoolmaster?
Did you ever marry?

truth.text: A neighbor back from the city says the schoolmaster lives on and even sits as a judge now.
lines:
It is true, an old farmer, who had been down to New York on a visit
several years after, and from whom this account of the ghostly adventure
was received, brought home the intelligence that Ichabod Crane was still
alive; that he had left the neighborhood partly through fear of the
goblin and Hans Van Ripper, and partly in mortification at having been
suddenly dismissed by the heiress; that he had changed his quarters to a
distant part of the country; had kept school and studied law at the same
time; had been admitted to the bar; turned politician; electioneered;
written for the newspapers; and finally had been made a justice of
the Ten Pound Court.

lie.text: I never married anyone from the valley. I'm still waiting for the right one.
lines:
Brom Bones, too, who, shortly after his rival’s
disappearance conducted the blooming Katrina in triumph to the altar,
was observed to look exceedingly knowing whenever the story of Ichabod
was related, and always burst into a hearty laugh at the mention of the
pumpkin; which led some to suspect that he knew more about the matter
than he chose to tell.

witnesses.caught: Oh, you know very well whom I married. I just like to keep people guessing.

world_map.art_description: An original hand-painted storybook map of the Sleepy Hollow countryside in New York's Hudson Valley around the year 1790, seen from above at a gentle three-quarter angle, at night under a bright full moon, lit by warm lantern and window glow. Deep indigo, violet and midnight-blue tones with amber and gold lights. Layout, which matters most: the broad Hudson River runs down the whole left edge of the picture, widening at the lower left into the wide Tappan Zee with one small moonlit sailboat. On the riverbank at the lower left, the small Dutch market village of Tarry Town with a tavern, a few houses and a little dock. On the riverbank at the upper left, the large prosperous Van Tassel farm: a long, low Dutch stone farmhouse with a deep front porch, a huge barn, an orchard, haystacks and a small spring under a great elm. In the center, a quiet green glen in a hollow between high wooded hills, with a small brook winding through it. In the lower center, a few small scattered farmhouses with lit windows and a little farm with a stable on the lower right. On the right side, near the bottom, a small log schoolhouse at the foot of a wooded hill beside the brook. A winding dirt road leaves the Van Tassel farm and runs to the right across the top of the map: beside it, standing alone, an enormous gnarled old tulip tree (top center); then a dark marshy swamp crossed by a small log bridge (top right); then the road curves down to a small white church on a knoll among trees on the right side, with a dark wooden bridge over the brook just below the church. Thinner roads link every place. Painterly and textured, rich but uncluttered, with wide areas of forest and hills between places. No people, no animals, no creatures, no ghosts. No text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no compass rose, no legend and no border.
